front: TIA or minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3): which antiplatelet plan, and for how long?
bottom: Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days, then one agent.

bullets.clue: High-risk TIA (ABCD2 ≥4) or minor stroke within 24 h.
bullets.treat: DAPT 21 days; high-intensity statin, LDL <70; BP control.
bullets.trap: Do not continue DAPT long term.

back: Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days, then one agent. Key clue: High-risk TIA (ABCD2 ≥4) or minor stroke within 24 h. First-line: DAPT 21 days; high-intensity statin, LDL <70; BP control. Exam trap: Do not continue DAPT long term.

diagram.alt: After high-risk TIA or minor stroke, aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days then a single antiplatelet, high-intensity statin to LDL under 70, carotid imaging and heart-rhythm monitoring.

source.guideline: 2021 AHA/ASA Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and TIA
source.recommendation: Noncardioembolic minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 ≥4) within 24 h: aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days, then single antiplatelet. Atherosclerotic stroke/TIA: high-intensity statin, LDL-C target <70 mg/dL; add ezetimibe then PCSK9 inhibitor if needed.

front: Spontaneous ICH vs aneurysmal SAH: the key BP target and the one drug for SAH?
bottom: ICH: lower SBP to 140. SAH: nimodipine.

bullets.clue: Thunderclap headache: SAH. Focal deficit, hypertension: ICH.
bullets.treat: ICH: SBP 140 (130–150), reverse anticoagulants. SAH: nimodipine 21 days, secure aneurysm.
bullets.trap: Do not drop ICH SBP below 130.

back: ICH: lower SBP to 140. SAH: nimodipine. Key clue: Thunderclap headache: SAH. Focal deficit, hypertension: ICH. First-line: ICH: SBP 140 (130–150), reverse anticoagulants. SAH: nimodipine 21 days, secure aneurysm. Exam trap: Do not drop ICH SBP below 130.

diagram.alt: Intracerebral hemorrhage: lower systolic BP to 140 and keep 130 to 150, reverse anticoagulation. Subarachnoid hemorrhage: nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days and early aneurysm repair.

source.guideline: 2022 AHA/ASA Spontaneous ICH Guideline; 2023 AHA/ASA Aneurysmal SAH Guideline
source.recommendation: ICH 2022: mild-moderate ICH with SBP 150–220: target 140, maintain 130–150; avoid <130. SAH 2023: enteral nimodipine to reduce delayed cerebral ischemia; nimodipine 60 mg q4h for 21 days.

front: Generalized seizure lasting 5 minutes: first drug, second drug, and timing?
bottom: Benzodiazepine at 5 minutes; second agent by 20–40.

bullets.clue: Seizure ≥5 minutes or no recovery between seizures.
bullets.treat: IV lorazepam or IM midazolam; then fosphenytoin, valproate or levetiracetam.
bullets.trap: Check glucose; do not under-dose benzodiazepines.

back: Benzodiazepine at 5 minutes; second agent by 20–40. Key clue: Seizure ≥5 minutes or no recovery between seizures. First-line: IV lorazepam or IM midazolam; then fosphenytoin, valproate or levetiracetam. Exam trap: Check glucose; do not under-dose benzodiazepines.

diagram.alt: Status epilepticus timeline: stabilize and check glucose, benzodiazepine at 5 minutes, then fosphenytoin, valproate or levetiracetam at 20 to 40 minutes, then anesthetic infusion with EEG.

source.guideline: AES Evidence-Based Guideline: Treatment of Convulsive Status Epilepticus (2016); AAN/AES Unprovoked First Seizure in Adults (2015)
source.recommendation: AES 2016: benzodiazepine at 5 min (IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg max 4 mg, IM midazolam 10 mg >40 kg, IV diazepam); 20–40 min: fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, valproate 40 mg/kg or levetiracetam 60 mg/kg; ESETT: no clear preferred second-line agent. AAN/AES 2015: recurrence 21–45% in 2 years; immediate AED reduces 2-year recurrence but not sustained remission.

front: Migraine vs cluster headache: first-line acute treatment, and which red flags need imaging?
bottom: Migraine: NSAID or triptan. Cluster: oxygen or sumatriptan.

bullets.clue: Cluster: unilateral orbital pain, tearing, attacks in bouts.
bullets.treat: Migraine: NSAID or triptan; gepant if triptans fail. Cluster: 100% oxygen or SC sumatriptan.

back: Migraine: NSAID or triptan. Cluster: oxygen or sumatriptan. Key clue: Cluster: unilateral orbital pain, tearing, attacks in bouts. First-line: Migraine: NSAID or triptan; gepant if triptans fail. Cluster: 100% oxygen or SC sumatriptan. Exam trap: Thunderclap or new after 50: image.

diagram.alt: Migraine treated with an NSAID then a triptan, gepants after triptan failure; cluster headache treated with 100 percent oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan; red flags such as thunderclap onset need imaging.

source.guideline: American Headache Society Consensus Statement: Integrating New Migraine Treatments (2021); AHS cluster oxygen statement
source.recommendation: AHS 2021: NSAIDs for mild-moderate attacks; triptans for moderate-severe; gepants or lasmiditan when triptans are contraindicated or after 2 failed triptans; limit acute medication. Cluster: oxygen 100% 6–12 L/min or SC sumatriptan 6 mg first-line acute therapy.

front: Resting tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia in a 72-year-old: first-line drug?

bullets.clue: Asymmetric resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, shuffling gait.
bullets.trap: Avoid dopamine agonists over 70 or with hallucinations.

back: Parkinson disease: start levodopa. Key clue: Asymmetric resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, shuffling gait. First-line: Carbidopa-levodopa, lowest effective dose. Exam trap: Avoid dopamine agonists over 70 or with hallucinations.

diagram.alt: Parkinson disease with resting tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia treated first with immediate-release levodopa; dopamine agonists only for selected patients under 60 and avoided over 70.

source.guideline: AAN Practice Guideline: Dopaminergic Therapy for Motor Symptoms in Early Parkinson Disease
source.recommendation: AAN 2021: levodopa preferred initial dopaminergic therapy at lowest effective dose; dopamine agonists may be considered for selected patients <60 at higher dyskinesia risk; avoid agonists in >70 or with impulse control disorders, cognitive impairment, sleepiness or hallucinations.

front: Acute confusion that fluctuates in a hospitalized 80-year-old vs slow memory loss: how to tell and treat?
bottom: Delirium is acute and fluctuating; dementia is gradual.

bullets.clue: Inattention and fluctuation point to delirium.
bullets.treat: Delirium: treat the cause, stop offending drugs. Dementia: check B12, TSH; cholinesterase inhibitor.
bullets.trap: Avoid benzodiazepines; antipsychotics only for danger.

back: Delirium is acute and fluctuating; dementia is gradual. Key clue: Inattention and fluctuation point to delirium. First-line: Delirium: treat the cause, stop offending drugs. Dementia: check B12, TSH; cholinesterase inhibitor. Exam trap: Avoid benzodiazepines; antipsychotics only for danger.

diagram.alt: Delirium is acute and fluctuating with inattention, screened with CAM and treated by finding the cause; dementia is gradual, worked up with B12 and TSH, and may use a cholinesterase inhibitor.

source.guideline: APA Practice Guideline for Prevention and Treatment of Delirium (2025); AGS Beers Criteria 2023; AAN Etiologic Diagnosis of Dementia
source.recommendation: Screen with CAM/4AT; treat reversible causes and review medications; avoid benzodiazepines (Beers) and routine antipsychotics, reserving them for severe distress or safety risk at the lowest dose and shortest duration. Dementia: check B12 and thyroid; cholinesterase inhibitors may be considered (avoid with syncope).

front: Optic neuritis, then numbness months later in a 30-year-old: diagnosis, relapse treatment and long-term plan?
bottom: Multiple sclerosis: MRI, steroids for relapse, early DMT.

bullets.clue: Neuro episodes separated in time and space; young woman.
bullets.treat: Relapse: IV methylprednisolone 3–5 days. Start disease-modifying therapy early.
bullets.trap: Steroids speed recovery but do not change long-term course.

back: Multiple sclerosis: MRI, steroids for relapse, early DMT. Key clue: Neuro episodes separated in time and space; young woman. First-line: Relapse: IV methylprednisolone 3–5 days. Start disease-modifying therapy early. Exam trap: Steroids speed recovery but do not change long-term course.

diagram.alt: Multiple sclerosis diagnosed with MRI under the 2024 McDonald criteria, relapses treated with high-dose methylprednisolone for 3 to 5 days, and disease-modifying therapy started early.

source.guideline: 2024 Revisions of the McDonald Criteria; AAN DMT Guideline (2018, reaffirmed 2024)
source.recommendation: McDonald 2024: optic nerve added as fifth location; central vein sign, paramagnetic rim lesions and CSF kappa free light chains may support diagnosis. AAN 2018 DMT guideline reaffirmed 2024. Relapse: methylprednisolone 1 g/day IV 3–5 days (review).

front: Ascending weakness after diarrhea vs fatigable ptosis: diagnosis and treatment?
bottom: GBS: IVIG or plasma exchange. MG: pyridostigmine.

bullets.clue: GBS: ascending weakness, lost reflexes. MG: worse with use.
bullets.treat: GBS: IVIG or plasma exchange; monitor vital capacity. MG: pyridostigmine; AChR antibodies.
bullets.trap: Do not give plasma exchange then IVIG.

back: GBS: IVIG or plasma exchange. MG: pyridostigmine. Key clue: GBS: ascending weakness, lost reflexes. MG: worse with use. First-line: GBS: IVIG or plasma exchange; monitor vital capacity. MG: pyridostigmine; AChR antibodies. Exam trap: Do not give plasma exchange then IVIG.

diagram.alt: Guillain-Barré syndrome with ascending weakness and lost reflexes treated with IVIG or plasma exchange and close breathing monitoring; myasthenia gravis with fatigable ptosis tested with AChR antibodies and treated with pyridostigmine.

source.guideline: EAN/PNS Guideline on Guillain-Barré Syndrome (2023); International Consensus Guidance for Myasthenia Gravis: 2020 Update
source.recommendation: EAN/PNS 2023: IVIg 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days within 2 weeks of onset in patients unable to walk unaided; PE within 4 weeks; equivalent; do not give PE immediately followed by IVIg. MG 2020: pyridostigmine symptomatic therapy.

front: Head injury with brief loss of consciousness, then a lucid interval: which bleed, and who needs CT?

bullets.clue: Lucid interval, temporal bone fracture, middle meningeal artery.
bullets.treat: Noncontrast head CT; neurosurgery for epidural.
bullets.trap: A lucid interval is unreliable; do not wait.

back: Epidural hematoma: lens-shaped; emergency surgery. Key clue: Lucid interval, temporal bone fracture, middle meningeal artery. First-line: Noncontrast head CT; neurosurgery for epidural. Exam trap: A lucid interval is unreliable; do not wait.

diagram.alt: Schematic heads: a lens-shaped epidural hematoma from the middle meningeal artery and a crescent subdural hematoma from bridging veins; head CT for GCS under 15 at 2 hours, age 65 or older, or repeated vomiting.

source.guideline: Canadian CT Head Rule; Brain Trauma Foundation Severe TBI 4th edition; CDC Pediatric mTBI Guideline (2018)
source.recommendation: Canadian CT Head Rule high-risk: GCS <15 at 2 h, suspected open/depressed fracture, basal skull fracture signs, vomiting ≥2, age ≥65. CDC 2018 pediatric mTBI: do not routinely image; use validated rules.

front: Vertigo on rolling over in bed vs continuous vertigo with skew deviation: peripheral or central?

bullets.clue: Brief positional vertigo with torsional nystagmus.
bullets.trap: HINTS: normal head impulse means central; image.

back: BPPV: Dix-Hallpike, then Epley. Key clue: Brief positional vertigo with torsional nystagmus. First-line: Epley maneuver; no vestibular suppressants. Exam trap: HINTS: normal head impulse means central; image.

diagram.alt: Positional vertigo diagnosed by Dix-Hallpike and treated with the Epley maneuver without vestibular suppressants; in continuous vertigo the HINTS exam finds central causes such as stroke.

source.recommendation: AAO-HNS 2017: diagnose posterior canal BPPV with Dix-Hallpike; treat with canalith repositioning; no post-procedure restrictions; do not routinely use vestibular suppressants. HINTS: normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew suggest central cause (review).

front: Morning headache with vomiting and papilledema: what is it, and what lowers the pressure?
bottom: Raised ICP from a mass: image, steroids if edema.

bullets.clue: Worse lying down, morning vomiting, papilledema.
bullets.treat: MRI with contrast; dexamethasone for symptomatic edema; neurosurgery.
bullets.trap: Cushing triad: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing.

back: Raised ICP from a mass: image, steroids if edema. Key clue: Worse lying down, morning vomiting, papilledema. First-line: MRI with contrast; dexamethasone for symptomatic edema; neurosurgery. Exam trap: Cushing triad: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing.

diagram.alt: Raised intracranial pressure from a brain mass with morning headache, vomiting and papilledema, imaged with contrast MRI and treated with dexamethasone only for symptomatic edema; Cushing triad warns of herniation.

source.guideline: CNS Guideline: Role of Steroids in Adults With Metastatic Brain Tumors; ASCO/SNO Joint Endorsement (2019)
source.recommendation: ASCO/SNO-endorsed CNS guideline: dexamethasone for symptomatic metastatic brain tumors with mass effect (4–8 mg/day mild; ≥16 mg/day severe), not for asymptomatic patients; no routine anticonvulsant prophylaxis.

front: Sudden one-sided facial droop including the forehead vs burning feet in diabetes: treatment?
bottom: Bell palsy: steroids within 72 h. Neuropathy pain: four drug classes.

bullets.treat: Bell: prednisone within 72 h; protect the eye. Neuropathy: gabapentinoid, SNRI, TCA or sodium-channel blocker.

back: Bell palsy: steroids within 72 h. Neuropathy pain: four drug classes. Key clue: Bell: whole face, forehead included. First-line: Bell: prednisone within 72 h; protect the eye. Neuropathy: gabapentinoid, SNRI, TCA or sodium-channel blocker. Exam trap: Forehead spared means central; image.

diagram.alt: Bell palsy involving the forehead treated with oral steroids within 72 hours and eye protection; painful diabetic neuropathy treated with gabapentinoids, SNRIs, tricyclics or sodium-channel blockers.

source.guideline: AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guideline: Bell's Palsy (2013); AAN Painful Diabetic Polyneuropathy Guideline Update (2022)
source.recommendation: AAO-HNS: oral steroids within 72 h for age ≥16; do not use antivirals alone; may add antivirals; eye protection if closure impaired. AAN 2022: TCAs, SNRIs, gabapentinoids and/or sodium-channel blockers for painful diabetic neuropathy.

front: Toddler with a brief generalized seizure during fever vs an infant with stiff legs: work-up?
bottom: Simple febrile seizure: no EEG or imaging. CP: diagnose early.

bullets.clue: Age 6 months–5 years, under 15 minutes, one per illness.
bullets.treat: Febrile: find the fever source. CP: MRI, HINE, General Movements.
bullets.trap: Meningeal signs need a lumbar puncture.

back: Simple febrile seizure: no EEG or imaging. CP: diagnose early. Key clue: Age 6 months–5 years, under 15 minutes, one per illness. First-line: Febrile: find the fever source. CP: MRI, HINE, General Movements. Exam trap: Meningeal signs need a lumbar puncture.

diagram.alt: Simple febrile seizure in a child 6 months to 5 years needs no EEG, blood work or imaging, with lumbar puncture only for meningeal signs; cerebral palsy is diagnosed early with MRI, General Movements Assessment and HINE.

source.guideline: AAP Febrile Seizures: Neurodiagnostic Evaluation of the Child With a Simple Febrile Seizure (2011); Early Diagnosis of Cerebral Palsy (Novak, JAMA Pediatrics 2017)
source.recommendation: AAP 2011: simple febrile seizure: no routine EEG, blood studies or neuroimaging; LP if meningeal signs, an option for 6–12 months if under-immunized or pretreated with antibiotics. Novak 2017: before 5 months, MRI, Prechtl GMA and HINE most predictive.
